claims.text: The starting protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC structure.
The as-cast coating has a relatively homogeneous microstructure with few initial nanoscale precipitates.
Thermal aging during or immediately before creep testing will stimulate formation of nanoscale BCC precipitates.
Nanoscale BCC precipitates form preferentially along grain boundaries.
The thermally induced precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Dynamic precipitation occurs under sustained stress and elevated temperature in the proposed coating.
The precipitates increase the barrier stress required for dislocation glide.
Precipitation-induced obstruction of dislocations produces a higher effective creep stress exponent.
Restricting dislocation mobility through precipitation reduces the creep strain rate and enhances creep resistance.
Thermally aged samples will have a lower creep strain rate than as-cast samples.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit a higher stress exponent than as-cast samples.
A higher stress exponent in the aged samples would indicate greater resistance to dislocation motion.
TEM will show a refined, precipitate-stabilized microstructure with precipitates concentrated at grain boundaries after aging.
Creep of the untreated as-cast coating is dominated by continuous dislocation motion with few intrinsic obstacles.
The proposed mechanism is effective during sustained high-temperature loading at constant stress.
Precipitate coarsening or dissolution at higher temperatures will diminish the creep-resistance benefit.
Applied stresses above a threshold will accelerate dislocation nucleation and diminish the benefit of precipitation.
The optimal precipitate size, spatial distribution, and volume fraction are unknown and may depend on alloy composition and service conditions.
